doc_description: This document presents a financial AI system designed to solve trust issues by rigorously verifying numerical data against SEC filings (via XBRL) and prose through exact matches or cosine similarity, using dual pipelines, strict refusal mechanisms, and structured query classification to eliminate hallucinations and ungrounded claims.

structure.title: The trust problem nobody solves
structure.text:
## The trust problem nobody solves Analysts, investors, and the merely curious all ask the same kind of question about public companies: *"What was Apple's R&D spend in FY2024?"* or *"What cybersecurity risks did Microsoft disclose in their latest 10-K?"* General-purpose assistants — Perplexity, ChatGPT — will happily answer. And in a financial-diligence context, that eagerness is exactly the problem. They fail in three ways that are all unacceptable when someone is about to make a decision on the answer: - **Hallucinated numbers.** A confidently-wrong revenue figure looks identical to a correct one. "Apple's R&D was ~$30B" — off by billions, no source. - **Ungrounded prose.** Risk factors get smoothed out of blended web sources rather than the actual filing. You get a paraphrase of a news article, not Item 1A. - **No refusal.** The model *always* answers, even when it has no business doing so. Ask about a company it has no data on and it invents a figure. ```mermaid flowchart LR Q["User question"] --> GP["Generic LLM
(Perplexity / ChatGPT)"] GP --> A1["Plausible answer"] A1 --> R1["❌ Number may be hallucinated"] A1 --> R2["❌ Source may be a web blog, not the filing"] A1 --> R3["❌ Never refuses — always answers"] ``` The core problem is *trust*. In diligence, a wrong-but-confident answer is worse than no answer, because you can't build on a number you can't verify. So I built an agent whose entire design goal is the opposite of "always be helpful": ground every claim in a specific SEC filing, or refuse.
structure.summary: The partial document addresses critical trust issues in using general-purpose AI assistants (e.g., Perplexity, ChatGPT) for financial diligence. It highlights three key failures: (1) **hallucinated numbers** (providing confidently incorrect financial figures without sources), (2) **ungrounded prose** (paraphrasing web content instead of citing direct SEC filings like 10-Ks), and (3) **unconditional answering** (generating responses even when lacking reliable data). The core problem is the inability to verify claims, which undermines decision-making in high-stakes contexts. The document introduces an alternative agent designed to prioritize trust by grounding all claims in specific SEC filings or explicitly refusing to answer when unverified.

structure.title: Making hallucination structural, not aspirational
structure.text:
## Making hallucination structural, not aspirational The interesting design constraint here is that "be more careful" is not a strategy. You can't prompt your way to zero hallucinations — at scale, *unlikely* still means *eventually*. The differentiation had to be **structural**: the architecture should make a hallucinated number *impossible*, not merely improbable. That comes down to three principles. **Numbers come from XBRL, never from prose.** Structured financial facts from `data.sec.gov` are the only source allowed to supply a numerical claim. The prose pipeline is *physically incapable* of putting a number into an answer — it never touches the numeric path. **Every prose claim is verified against its source chunk.** A dedicated `cite_check` step confirms each sentence actually appears in (or is cosine-similar to) the retrieved filing text before it ships. **Refuse rather than guess.** No ticker, no grounding, out-of-scope concept? The agent returns a refusal — HTTP 200 with `refused=true` — not a fabricated answer. ```mermaid flowchart LR Q["User question"] --> AG["SEC 10-K Agent"] AG --> P1["XBRL pipeline
(structured facts)"] AG --> P2["Prose pipeline
(vector search + cite-check)"] P1 --> N["Numbers — exact-match verified ✅"] P2 --> T["Prose — substring/cosine verified ✅"] AG --> X["No grounding? → Refuse, don't guess ✅"] N --> ANS["Answer with verifiable citation"] T --> ANS ``` Every tradeoff downstream is made through one lens: *can I defend this answer against the question "where did that come from?"* If I can't, the agent shouldn't say it.
structure.summary: The partial document outlines a structural approach to preventing hallucinations in an AI system processing SEC filings. It emphasizes three core principles: (1) numerical data must exclusively derive from structured XBRL financial data, not prose; (2) all prose claims must be verified against source text via exact matches or cosine similarity checks; (3) the system must explicitly refuse to answer when lacking grounding in the data. A flowchart illustrates the dual pipeline architecture—structured XBRL and prose verification—with a refusal pathway for ungrounded queries. The focus is on making hallucinations architecturally impossible through strict source validation and rejection of speculative outputs.

structure.title: Four kinds of question, two kinds of answer
structure.text:
## Four kinds of question, two kinds of answer

The first thing the agent does is classify the incoming question into one of four types. Only two of them are allowed to produce a grounded answer.

**Type A — Numerical lookup.** Single company, single period, single metric. *"Apple's R&D in FY2024?"* This runs `plan → fetch → retrieve(XBRL) → validate → cite_check`, and it's restricted to a **10-item whitelist** of us-gaap concepts. No fuzzy tag matching — the question maps to exactly one key or it refuses.

**Type B — Qualitative single-filing.** Risk or strategy prose from one filing. *"Microsoft's cybersecurity risks?"* This runs `plan → fetch → locate → retrieve(vector) → validate → cite_check`, restricted to **Item 1A, Item 7, and Item 8** — the sections with the cleanest boundaries.

**META.** Greetings, thanks, "what can you do?", chitchat. Handled by a concierge node that never answers a domain question.

**REFUSE.** Everything else — no ticker, year-over-year, cross-company, a non-whitelisted concept, a non-10-K source, off-topic. HTTP 200 with `refused=true`.

A subtle but important choice: **META is kept separate from REFUSE.** They could collapse into one "didn't answer" bucket, but then your evals and dashboards would conflate *"the user said hi"* with *"we couldn't ground an answer"* — and those mean completely different things about system health.

The Type A whitelist is what makes the "zero hallucination" promise concrete. The `plan` node maps user phrasing to exactly one of these keys, or it refuses:

```
revenue       → Revenues / RevenueFromContractWithCustomerExcludingAssessedTax
net_income    → NetIncomeLoss
rnd           → ResearchAndDevelopmentExpense
total_assets  → Assets
total_debt    → LongTermDebt            (MVP: long-term only)
cash          → CashAndCashEquivalentsAtCarryingValue
eps_diluted   → EarningsPerShareDiluted
shares_out    → CommonStockSharesOutstanding
opex          → OperatingExpenses
gross_profit  → GrossProfit
```

And the non-goals are explicit on purpose: international filings, real-time prices, earnings transcripts, filings older than 2015, year-over-year comparisons, cross-company queries — all deferred. The interesting part is that **YoY and cross-company questions ship as *known refusals* in an adversarial eval set.** A clean refusal you can point to is a stronger story than a half-built feature that sometimes works.
structure.summary:
The partial document outlines a system for classifying and handling user queries in a financial data retrieval framework. Key points include:  
1. **Four Query Types**:  
   - **Type A (Numerical Lookup)**: Single-company, single-period, single-metric queries (e.g., "Apple's R&D in FY2024"). Requires strict mapping to a 10-item GAAP concept whitelist, ensuring "zero hallucinations" by rejecting ambiguous matches.  
   - **Type B (Qualitative Single-Filing)**: Risk/strategy prose from specific filing sections (e.g., "Microsoft's cybersecurity risks"). Limited to Items 1A, 7, and 8 of filings.  
   - **META**: Handles greetings, system inquiries, and non-domain questions via a dedicated "concierge" node.  
   - **REFUSE**: Rejects invalid queries (e.g., cross-company, year-over-year, non-whitelisted concepts) with explicit refusal signals.  

2. **Design Decisions**:  
   - **Separation of META and REFUSE**: Maintains distinct metrics for system evaluation, avoiding conflating user greetings with query rejection.  
   - **Whitelist Enforcement**: Type A’s rigid 10-item GAAP mapping ensures precision, while Type B uses vector retrieval for structured sections.  
   - **Non-Goals**: Explicitly defers international filings, real-time data, earnings transcripts, and older filings (<2015).  

3. **Adversarial Evaluation**:  
   - Known refusals (e.g., YoY, cross-company queries) are intentionally included in evaluation sets to validate clean rejection boundaries, prioritizing reliability over partial feature implementation.  

The document emphasizes structured, grounded answers for specific query types while maintaining strict boundaries to avoid unsupported outputs.

structure.title: Two pipelines, one agent
structure.text:
## Two pipelines, one agent Underneath, two parallel data pipelines feed a single LangGraph agent. The split between them is load-bearing — it's the whole reason numbers can't leak from prose. ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph Ingestion["Ingestion (one-shot, pre-warm)"] EDGAR["SEC EDGAR
(HTML + data.sec.gov)"] EDGAR --> EC["edgar_client.py
5 req/s token bucket"] EC --> PARSE["parser.py
edgartools section extract
(Item 1A / 7 / 8)"] PARSE --> CHUNK["chunker.py
~500-token sliding window"] CHUNK --> EMBED["embedder.py
text-embedding-3-small"] EC --> XBRLF["xbrl.py
company-facts JSON → rows"] end subgraph DB["Postgres + pgvector (single instance)"] CHUNKS[("chunks
VECTOR(1536) + HNSW")] FACTS[("xbrl_facts
NUMERIC(28,4)")] QLOG[("query_log")] ACACHE[("answer_cache")] end EMBED --> CHUNKS XBRLF --> FACTS subgraph Agent["LangGraph Agent (per /ask)"] GRAPH["plan → fetch → locate →
retrieve → validate → cite_check"] end CHUNKS --> GRAPH FACTS --> GRAPH GRAPH --> QLOG GRAPH --> ACACHE subgraph Serve["Serving"] FE["Next.js (Vercel)
+ Clerk auth"] API["FastAPI /ask /companies /health"] end User(["User"]) --> FE FE -->|"server-side proxy
(holds API key / Clerk JWT)"| API API --> GRAPH ``` The **prose pipeline** takes EDGAR HTML, extracts the relevant Item sections with edgartools, slices them into ~500-token sliding-window chunks, embeds those with OpenAI's `text-embedding-3-small`, and stores them in pgvector. Retrieval is cosine similarity *restricted to the relevant Item section of one company* — never a free-for-all over the whole corpus. The **XBRL pipeline** pulls structured rows straight from `data.sec.gov`'s company-facts JSON. The agent queries this directly for any number. Prose chunks are never consulted for a numeric answer. The `plan` node is the switch that decides which pipeline a question takes. That single routing decision is the mechanism that makes hallucinated numbers structurally impossible — a number can only come from a path that has no prose in it.
structure.summary:
The partial document describes a system architecture with two distinct data pipelines feeding a single LangGraph agent to process financial data from the SEC's EDGAR database. Key components include:

1. **Prose Pipeline**: 
   - Extracts HTML content from SEC filings (EDGAR), focusing on specific sections (e.g., Item 1A/7/8).
   - Processes text via chunking (~500-token sliding window), embedding (OpenAI's `text-embedding-3-small`), and stores in a vector database (Postgres + pgvector) for similarity search.
   - Used exclusively for qualitative prose-based answers.

2. **XBRL Pipeline**: 
   - Parses structured numeric data from `data.sec.gov` (company-facts JSON) into relational rows.
   - Stores numeric values in a Postgres table for direct querying.
   - Ensures numeric answers derive solely from structured XBRL data, preventing "leakage" from unstructured prose.

3. **LangGraph Agent**: 
   - Routes queries via a `plan` node to select the appropriate pipeline.
   - Executes a workflow (plan → fetch → locate → retrieve → validate → cite_check) to generate answers.
   - Logs queries and caches answers for efficiency.

4. **Architecture**: 
   - Separates ingestion (one-shot pre-processing) from serving (FastAPI/Next.js).
   - Uses Postgres + pgvector for hybrid storage of vectorized prose and structured numeric data.
   - Enforces strict data isolation to prevent hallucinations: numbers cannot originate from prose chunks.

structure.title: The agent graph
structure.text:
## The agent graph The agent itself is six nodes sharing one typed Pydantic `AgentState` — think of it as a clipboard. Each node reads specific fields and appends its own outputs; nodes never mutate what an earlier node wrote. That immutability makes the whole run traceable after the fact. ```mermaid flowchart TD plan["plan
(cheap LLM, structured out)"] plan -->|Type A| retrieveA["retrieve (XBRL)"] plan -->|Type B| locate["locate"] plan -->|META| concierge["concierge → END"] plan -->|REFUSE| refuse["refusal_composer → END"] locate --> retrieveB["retrieve (vector, top-8)"] retrieveA --> cacheA{"cache hit?"} retrieveB --> cacheB{"cache hit?"} cacheA -->|hit| ENDc["END (skip validate)"] cacheB -->|hit| ENDc cacheA -->|miss| validate["validate
(frontier LLM, structured out)"] cacheB -->|miss| validate validate --> citecheck["cite_check
(deterministic verify)"] citecheck -->|verified| END(["END"]) citecheck -->|any claim fails| refuse fetchfail["fetch / locate / retrieve / validate
refuse paths"] -.-> refuse ``` Each node has a tight contract — what it reads, what it writes, and the exact conditions under which it bails to a refusal: - **plan** (cheap LLM): reads the question, writes the type, ticker, CIK, fiscal year, and concept/item. Refuses if there's no ticker, it can't classify, the concept isn't whitelisted, or the item isn't 1A/7/8. - **fetch** (plain SQL): resolves the filing. Refuses if the company isn't in the universe or the year wasn't ingested. - **locate** (SQL): finds the section. Refuses if it wasn't parsed. - **retrieve**: pulls the XBRL fact (Type A) or the top chunks (Type B). Refuses on no fact / zero hits. - **validate** (frontier LLM): drafts the answer and emits discrete claims. Refuses if it can't produce grounded claims. - **cite_check** (deterministic, no LLM): verifies every claim against its source. Refuses if any claim fails. There's a deliberate **cost-discipline move** in the model tiering: cheap models (Haiku, GPT-4o-mini) drive `plan` and `locate`, and only `validate` — the one node that actually writes prose a human will read — uses a frontier model. The whole thing targets under $20/month to operate.
structure.summary:
The partial document describes an **agent graph** workflow for processing queries, emphasizing **modular nodes**, **immutability**, and **cost efficiency**. Key components include:  

1. **Agent Graph Structure**:  
   - Six nodes share a read-only `AgentState` (like a clipboard), ensuring traceability through immutability.  
   - Nodes handle specific tasks (planning, retrieval, validation) and transition based on input types (Type A/B, META, REFUSE).  

2. **Node Functions**:  
   - **`plan`**: Uses a cheap LLM to classify queries, extract parameters (ticker, concept), and route to subsequent nodes. Refuses invalid queries.  
   - **`retrieve`**: Fetches XBRL data (Type A) or vector-based chunks (Type B), with caching to skip validation on cache hits.  
   - **`validate`**: Employs a high-cost "frontier" LLM to generate answers and structured claims, rejecting ungrounded responses.  
   - **`cite_check`**: Deterministically verifies claims against sources, triggering refusal if any claim fails.  

3. **Cost Optimization**:  
   - Cheap models (e.g., Haiku, GPT-4o-mini) handle planning and locating to minimize expenses.  
   - Only the `validate` node uses an expensive frontier model, targeting under $20/month operational costs.  

4. **Refusal Paths**:  
   - Nodes exit to a `refusal_composer` if inputs are invalid, data is missing, or claims fail verification.  

5. **Traceability**:  
   - Immutable state updates and structured outputs enable post-hoc auditing of the workflow.  

The design balances efficiency, accuracy, and cost control for query processing in financial or structured data contexts.

structure.title: The two guards that do the real work
structure.text:
## The two guards that do the real work

Everything above is plumbing. The part that actually earns trust is the verification, and it splits cleanly along the same numbers-vs-prose line.

nodes.title: Guard 1: numbers verified by exact match
nodes.text:
### Guard 1: numbers verified by exact match ```mermaid flowchart LR V["validate node
formats $3,540,000,000"] --> C["cite_check"] C --> P["parse number from claim.text"] P --> EQ{"== xbrl_fact.value?
(no tolerance)"} EQ -->|yes| OK["✅ claim verified"] EQ -->|no| FAIL["❌ refuse — signals upstream bug"] ``` There is **no tolerance band**. The number the agent writes must exactly equal the XBRL fact it claims to cite. This feels aggressive until you think about what a mismatch actually means: it's never a legitimate rounding difference worth hiding, it's a bug worth surfacing. A tolerance window would just paper over the exact failures you most want to catch.

nodes.title: Guard 2: prose verified by a three-tier check
nodes.text:
### Guard 2: prose verified by a three-tier check

Prose is fuzzier, so verification escalates through three tiers, each catching a different failure mode:

1. **Verbatim substring of the cited chunk** — the normal, happy case.
2. **Verbatim substring of *any* retrieved chunk** — catches the LLM citing the wrong `source_idx` while still saying something true.
3. **Cosine ≥ 0.85 between the evidence quote and a chunk** — catches paraphrasing despite instructions not to.

And one pragmatic escape hatch that mattered a lot in practice: **partial answers.** If at most a third of the claims fail and at least one passes, the failing sentences are dropped and the verified portion is returned. That single change took the false-refusal rate from 11.8% down to 0% — a reminder that an all-or-nothing verifier punishes the user for the model's worst sentence.

structure.title: Finding the right prose in the first place
structure.text:
## Finding the right prose in the first place

Verification only helps if retrieval surfaced the right text to begin with. Naive cosine search wasn't good enough, so Type B retrieval stacks four improvements:

**Hybrid search with RRF.** A semantic search (cosine on embeddings) and a keyword search (Postgres `ts_rank`, BM25-style) run independently and get fused with Reciprocal Rank Fusion — `score = Σ 1 / (60 + rank)`. RRF sidesteps the scale-mismatch headache of trying to weight two incomparable score distributions into a linear sum.

**Multi-query decomposition.** A compound question like "cybersecurity *and* competition risks" gets split into two or three focused sub-queries. Each runs the full hybrid search, and the results are merged with an outer RRF, capped at 8 chunks.

**Contextual embeddings.** Each chunk is embedded with a filing-context prefix — `Microsoft (MSFT) 10-K FY2024 — Item 1A Risk Factors: <text>` — to close the vocabulary gap between how people ask questions and how filings phrase things.

**Year-scoped retrieval.** When a year is specified, search is filtered to that filing's accession number, so a newer filing can't contaminate an older-year answer.
structure.summary:
The partial document outlines four key improvements in Type B retrieval to enhance the accuracy of finding relevant text in documents like financial filings. The main points are:  
1. **Hybrid Search with RRF**: Combines semantic (embedding-based cosine) and keyword (BM25-style) searches, fused via Reciprocal Rank Fusion to avoid scale mismatches.  
2. **Multi-Query Decomposition**: Splits complex queries (e.g., "cybersecurity and competition risks") into sub-queries, each processed with hybrid search and merged via RRF, capped at 8 results.  
3. **Contextual Embeddings**: Prefixes chunks with metadata (e.g., "Microsoft (MSFT) 10-K FY2024 — Item 1A Risk Factors") to align user queries with filing-specific phrasing.  
4. **Year-Scoped Retrieval**: Filters results by filing year using accession numbers to prevent newer filings from influencing older-year answers.  
These methods aim to address retrieval challenges like vocabulary gaps, query complexity, and temporal contamination.

structure.title: Storage: one database, idempotent by design
structure.text:
## Storage: one database, idempotent by design

All of this lives in a single Postgres instance with pgvector. Five tables, every one keyed on SEC's own natural identifiers (CIK, accession number) so that re-ingesting a filing is idempotent rather than duplicative.

```mermaid
erDiagram
    companies ||--o{ filings : "has"
    filings ||--o{ chunks : "extracted into"
    companies ||--o{ xbrl_facts : "reports"
    filings ||--o{ xbrl_facts : "cited by"

    companies {
        char cik PK
        text ticker UK
        text name
        text sic
    }
    filings {
        text accession_no PK
        char cik FK
        date filing_date
        int fiscal_year
        text ingestion_status
    }
    chunks {
        bigserial id PK
        text accession_no FK
        char cik
        text item "1A | 7 | 8"
        text text
        vector embedding "VECTOR(1536) + HNSW"
        int char_start
        int char_end
    }
    xbrl_facts {
        bigserial id PK
        char cik FK
        text concept "us-gaap tag"
        numeric value "NUMERIC(28,4)"
        int fiscal_year
        text accession_no FK "citation source"
    }
    query_log {
        bigserial id PK
        text request_id
        text question_type
        int latency_ms
        boolean refused
    }
```

Two more tables round it out: an `answer_cache` for exact-match LLM answer caching, and an optional LangGraph checkpointer table for opt-in conversation memory. Using one Postgres instance for prose, facts, cache, and checkpointer isn't a compromise at this scale — it's the right call, and it fits on a free tier.
structure.summary:
The partial document describes a database architecture designed for SEC filings and financial data, emphasizing a single Postgres instance with pgvector for vector storage. Key components include five core tables: `companies`, `filings`, `chunks`, `xbrl_facts`, and `query_log`, all keyed on SEC identifiers (CIK, accession number) to ensure idempotent re-ingestion of data. The schema supports:  
1. **Idempotent storage** via natural keys to prevent duplicates.  
2. **Vector embeddings** in `chunks` for text analysis (e.g., SEC filing sections like "Item 1A").  
3. **XBRL financial facts** linked to companies and filings, storing concepts (e.g., "us-gaap tags") and numeric values.  
4. **Query logging** for tracking search performance and outcomes.  
Additional tables (`answer_cache`, LangGraph checkpointer) enable LLM answer caching and conversation memory. The design prioritizes scalability and simplicity, leveraging Postgres' capabilities to handle prose, structured facts, and vector data efficiently, even on a free-tier instance.

structure.title: A request, end to end
structure.text:
## A request, end to end Here's what actually happens when someone asks a question — including the part where the API key never touches the browser: ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant U as Browser participant FE as Next.js /api/ask (Vercel) participant API as FastAPI /ask participant G as LangGraph Agent participant DB as Postgres+pgvector U->>FE: POST {question} Note over FE: attach Clerk JWT / X-API-Key
(key never reaches browser) FE->>API: POST /ask (+ identity) Note over API: resolve Identity(tier, key)
token-budget + rate-limit check API->>G: run graph G->>DB: plan→fetch→locate→retrieve DB-->>G: xbrl_fact / chunks G->>DB: answer_cache lookup alt cache hit DB-->>G: cached answer else cache miss G->>G: validate (frontier LLM) G->>G: cite_check (verify every claim) end G-->>API: {answer, claims, verified, refused} API->>DB: write query_log API-->>FE: JSON (or SSE stream) FE-->>U: rendered answer + citations ``` The frontend is a server-side proxy: it holds the API key and the Clerk JWT, so neither ever reaches the user's browser. On the API side, every request resolves to an `Identity(tier, key)`: - **`tier="user"`** — a valid Clerk JWT verified against Clerk's JWKS. A present-but-invalid token is a hard **401**, never a silent downgrade to anonymous. - **`tier="anon"`** — everything else, keyed by remote IP. Those tiers carry different budgets. Anonymous users get 5 requests and 5,000 tokens per minute with a 1,000-token input cap; signed-in users get 60 requests, 50,000 tokens, and 2,000. Both are in-process sliding windows (single replica), and anonymous users additionally have a lifetime per-IP cap and a ticker allowlist. The `413` and `429` responses share one shape — `reason`, `auth_required`, and a `limit` object — so the frontend can branch cleanly between "show the sign-in modal" and "show a toast."
structure.summary:
The partial document outlines the end-to-end workflow of handling a user query in a system integrating frontend, API, and backend components. Key points include:  
1. **Request Flow**: A sequence diagram showing the browser sending a POST request to a Next.js API, which proxies to a FastAPI backend. The FastAPI triggers a LangGraph agent to process the query, interacting with a Postgres+pgvector database for data retrieval, caching, and validation.  
2. **Security**: The frontend acts as a server-side proxy, ensuring API keys and Clerk JWTs never reach the browser. Identity resolution uses Clerk's JWT verification for authenticated users (`tier="user"`) or IP-based anonymous access (`tier="anon"`).  
3. **Rate Limiting & Budgets**: Authenticated users receive higher token and request limits (60 requests, 50k tokens) compared to anonymous users (5 requests, 5k tokens). Both tiers use sliding-window rate limiting, with additional IP-based caps for anonymous users.  
4. **Processing Logic**: The LangGraph agent performs steps like plan→fetch→locate→retrieve, checks a cache, and validates answers using an LLM and citation verification.  
5. **Error Handling**: Standardized `413`/`429` responses provide structured feedback (e.g., `reason`, `auth_required`) to differentiate between authentication prompts and rate-limit toasts.  
6. **Logging**: Query logs are written to the database for tracking.

structure.title: Knowing when to stop
structure.text:
## Knowing when to stop

The thing I'm proudest of isn't a clever retrieval trick — it's the definition of done. The quality bar is wired into CI as a *failing gate*, not a vibe:

- A public URL answering in under 5 seconds, with citations.
- An eval harness with ≥30 golden questions, ≥85% citation accuracy, **0 numeric tripwire failures**, and a <5% claim-level unsupported rate.
- Live production traces in a Langfuse dashboard.

The gate is deliberately the **two split components** — the numeric tripwire and the claim-level unsupported rate — rather than a single headline "hallucination rate." A blended metric hides which half is broken. The evals also track Recall@5 and Recall@8 as diagnostics, because they disambiguate the two ways a false refusal can happen: Recall@5 = 0 means retrieval failed to surface the answer; Recall@5 = 1 means retrieval found it and validate/cite_check threw it away. Those point at completely different fixes.

Everything is sized for portfolio-demo scale — 50 companies, ~150 filings, 15–22k vector rows, a handful of concurrent users — and the non-goals are stated as loudly as the goals: no sharded Postgres, no Kubernetes, no Redis, no managed vector DB. The one real bottleneck is SEC's rate limit, and it only binds during a one-shot ingestion that the user never sees.

That, in the end, is the whole thesis. The hard part of a diligence agent isn't getting it to answer — any model does that. The hard part is building one that knows the difference between an answer it can defend and one it can't, and has the discipline to stay quiet about the second kind.
structure.summary:
The partial document outlines the criteria and design principles for a system that ensures reliable, defensible answers in a diligence agent. Key points include:  
1. **Definition of Done**: A quality bar enforced as a CI failing gate, requiring a public URL with sub-5-second response times, citations, and an evaluation harness with strict metrics (≥30 golden questions, ≥85% citation accuracy, 0 numeric tripwire failures, <5% unsupported claims).  
2. **Evaluation Metrics**: Dual focus on numeric tripwire failures and claim-level unsupported rates to avoid obscuring issues in a blended "hallucination rate." Additional diagnostics like Recall@5 and Recall@8 help identify retrieval failures or validation errors.  
3. **System Constraints**: Designed for portfolio-demo scale (50 companies, ~150 filings), explicitly excluding complex infrastructure (no sharded Postgres, Kubernetes, Redis, or managed vector DB). The SEC's rate limit is the primary bottleneck during ingestion.  
4. **Core Thesis**: The challenge lies not in generating answers but in distinguishing between defensible and indefensible responses, with the system disciplined to avoid providing unsupported claims.
